title: What do candidates say about real consulting interviews?
description: Common themes from candidates' published interview experiences at MBB, the Big Four and Accenture: formats, surprises and lessons.
hook: Reading other people's interview experiences can calm a lot of nerves, because it turns the unknown into something familiar. We read through candidates' published reports and prep guides and pulled out the patterns that come up again and again. Individual experiences vary, so treat these as themes, not rules.
body:
Formats are fairly consistent

  • Bain: candidates often describe first rounds of two back-to-back interviews of around 45 minutes, each with a case and fit questions, and later rounds with managers and partners.
  • Deloitte: many describe a mix of online assessments, a group exercise and individual case or competency interviews.
  • Accenture: candidates often report rounds pairing a case with a behavioural interview, followed by a more conversational final chat with a senior leader.
  • McKinsey: every interview combines a case with a deep personal experience conversation.

Interviewers are often kinder than expected

Many candidates describe interviewers as friendly, supportive and willing to guide them through the case. A hint is not a trap; use it.

Fit questions matter more than people expect

Candidates who prepared only cases often say the fit or experience questions were where they struggled. Prepare stories with real detail.

Feedback varies

Some firms give feedback quickly, sometimes the same or next day after a round. Others give little. If you are rejected, ask politely for feedback; you may get useful pointers. What to do after a rejection.

Timelines vary a lot

Reported processes range from a few days for campus rounds to several months for experienced hires. Ask your recruiter what to expect.

Sources

  • Glassdoor: Bain interview reviews
  • Glassdoor: Bain interview reviews (campus)
  • Glassdoor: Deloitte graduate consultant interviews
  • Glassdoor: Accenture strategy interviews

Checked November 2026.

How to learn from interview reports without overfitting

Candidate reports are useful for learning the range of formats, common case types and the intensity of follow-up questions. They are less reliable as a forecast of the exact questions you will receive. An experience shared by a recent graduate in one country may describe a completely different process from a senior-hire position elsewhere.

When reading a report, extract only transferable behaviours. Did the candidate have to clarify ambiguous goals? Was their arithmetic challenged? Did the interviewer switch topics without warning? Could they give a concise recommendation from incomplete data? Then practise those behaviours using an unfamiliar original case, not the same questions word for word.

Create a one-page interview debrief after each of your own rounds, while memories are fresh. Record what you were asked, where you needed to slow down, which data you requested and what you would do differently. Treat vague social-media claims about "secret frameworks" or guaranteed interviews with scepticism. Your own repeated performance patterns are stronger evidence for the next preparation step.
